full_judgment:
2. Respondent No.1 filed the Misc. case for pre-emption of a land sold under a Kabala dated 18-6-70 alleging that he was a co-sharer of the land but was not given any notice of the transfer to a stranger. The transferee; who is the appellant here, contested the application contending, among, other things, that the application suffered from defect of parties in that a number of co-sharers by inheritance were not impleaded in the application for pre-emotion. The learned Munsif infected this contention holding that the omission of certain persons as referred to in section 96(2) was not fatal to the proceeding and allowed the pre-emption. On appeal the learned Subordinate lodge found that a number of co-sharers by inheritance were notes pleaded even after objection was taken by the pre-emptee at the earliest opportunity and held that this nova joinder of parts was fatal to the proceeding and on such findings reversed the Munsif's order. In revision under section 115, Civil Procedure Code the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division relying upon the decision of this Division in Motilal Sikdar Vs. Binodini Dasi 28 DLR (AD) 5 held that the cleft out co-sharers were not necessary parties as they got no subsisting interests in the land transferred end as such the defect of parties was not fatal to the proceeding. 

 3. In this appeal the question raised is whether in the light of the decision in Motilal Sikdar's case as clarified by a subsequent decision in the case of Abdus Samad vs. Sohrab A. (1981) 33 DLR (AD) 113 the High Court Division was well founded in law to hold that the left out co-sharers of the pre-emptor had no subsisting right of pre-emption and as such the non-joinder of parties was not fatal to tire proceeding. 

 "It does not appear from a perusal of the provision of section 96 that it was the intent of the legislature that the penalty for non-impleading a person as contemplated in subsection (2) is the invalidity of the order which may ultimately be made in the said proceeding. The question whether a person it a necessary party under sub-section (2) is a question of fact and the object of this provision seems to provide the co-sharer tenants and the holders of the contiguous lands with the opportunity of availing of the provision of the said subsection. Since the benefit conferred under the said provisions is meant for certain individuals; they can very well be waived. In that view of the matter the positive injunction contained in the said sub-section as to the making of parties in spite of its being couched in mandatory language should be read as directory”. 

 9. Facts in the ease of Abdus Samad Vs. Sohrabali are that the petition for pre-emption was filed by a non-notified co-sharer but It was opposed on the ground that many other co-sharers by inheritance were not impleaded and that though this objection was raised at the earliest possible opportunity the defect was not rectified. The trial court allowed the pre-emption disregarding the objection, but the lower appellate court set aside the pre-emption and dismissed the application for pre-emption holding that the defect of patties was fatal to the proceeding. The High Court Division, however, relying upon the decision in Motilal Sikder's case allowed the pre-emption holding that the requirement for impleading the co-sharer or contiguous land-holders as referred to In section 96 (2) is not mandatory but is merely directory. This Division, on appeal, held that the defect of parties was fatal to the proceeding of Pre-emption and that the ratio decidendi of Motilal Sikder's case was not properly appreciated and correctly applied by the High Court Division. 

 10. In the instant case the land transferred originally belonged to one Barku who died leaving five sons, three daughters and two widows. Aushi Bali is one of the daughters on whore death her son Jainuddin and daughter Jarunnessa inherited her share and at the time of the transfer to question they were alive but were not impleaded in the pre-emption cage Afzau Bibi was another daughter of Barku. She died leaving four sons including Momtaj on whos death his two sons Karamat Ali and Giasuddin inherited his share but they were not impleaded in the proceeding. Again, one Sahera, grand-daughter of Elahi who was the 4th son of Barku, though admittedly a co-sharer was not impleaded. The explanation for non-joinder of parties on such a large scale was that the pre-emptee objector did not furnish the names and particulars of the left-out co-sharers under an affidavit though he was directed to do so by the trial court. It appears that when obj clan was raised as to defect of parties at the earliest possible opportunity the pre-emptor submitted to the pre-emptee an interrogatory asking him to furnish the names and particulars of the left-out co-sharers. Those particulars were in fact furnished accordingly but without an affidavit. The trial court at the instance of the pre-emptor rejected the objection as to defect of parties holding the pre-emptor objector was responsible for the omission and allowed the pre-emption. The order for pre-emption was set aside in appeal by the learned Subordinate Judge who held that the objector pre-emptee was under no legal obligation to furnish by affidavit the names and particulars of the let out co-sharers and that the non-joinder of parties was fatal to the pre-emption proceeding As against this order, the High Court was moved by an application under section 115 Civil Procedure Code in which a ground was taken that the left out to sharers had no subsisting right of pre-emption and as such their omission was not fats to the proceeding. The High Court Division accepted this contention observing that "it does not appear that there is anything on record to indicate that the alleged left-out heirs of Barka bad a subsisting right of pre-emption." 

 11. Mr Anil Chandra Sarker, learned Advocate for the appellant has contended that it was for the pre-emptor to lead evidence showing that the left-out co-sharers had lost their interest in the laud in question by transfer or otherwise and that the High Court Division shitted the burden of proof upon the pre-emptee in this respect. It is not disputed that the left-out persons are co-sharers by inheritance. But there is no evidence whatever to show that they got no subsisting interest in the land under pre-emption. Mr. Yeasin, the learned Advocate for the respondent, has failed to show us how it could be held that the left-out co-sharers lost or transferred their interest in the land under pre-emption. The onus of proof in this respect is upon the pre-emptor but this onus has not been discharged. The observation of the High Court Division as quoted above shows that it was for the pre-emptee to lead evidence to the effect that the left out co-sharers still get interest in the land sought to be  pre-emptee The High Court Division in this connection relied upon the decision in Motilal Sikder's case in which it was observed that the positive injunction as to parties under section 96 (2) is directory. The facts of this case as set out above are not attracted by the decision in Motilal's case ; on the contrary, these facts are attracted by the decision in the case of Abdus Scoriae vs. Sohrab Ali an which it has been held that non-joinder of parties who got right of preemption is fatal to the proceeding". 

 12. In Motilal Sikdar's case it was observed that the question as to joinder of parties Is essentially a matter of procedure and that this procedure has been laid down in Order 1, Civil Procedure Code. It was further observed that by virtue of section 141 of this Code the provisions of Order 1 are applicable to a pre-emption proceeding which is of original nature Rule 9 of Order 1, C.P. Code provides that "no suit shall be defeated by reason of the mis-joinder or non-joinder of parties and the court may in every suit deal with the matter in controversy so far as regards the rights and interests of the parties actually before it". In the said case, the left out contiguous land owner lost the contiguity between his land and the land transferred after the partition with his brother. In that back ground it was observed by this Division that the provision as to Parties under section 90 (2) is merely directory. It may be "stated here for clarification that though the provisions of Order 1, Civil Procedure Code are applicable to a pre-emption proceeding, this provision is subject to the special provision of section 96 (2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 13. Mr. Anil Chandra Sarker, the learned Advocate has in this. connection referred to an observation of the then High Court of East Pakistan in the case of "Syed Abdul Karim vs. Harendra Chondra Dhupi, 14 DLR, 847 Which is to the effect that the provision as to joinder of parties in a suit for partition is the same as that in a suit for pre-emption" since in both the cases the presence of the necessary parties is Indispensably required not only as a matter or convenience but also to enable the court to adjudicate more effectively and completely. The decision in that case Syed Abdul Karim vs. Harendra Chandra Dhupi, was referred to in the judgment of Motilal Sikder's case. We however see. no necessity to draw any such analogy between a partition suit and a pre-emption case as to the making of parties in that the provision as to parties in a partition suit is governed by Order 1, rule 10, C. P. Code whereas the provision as to parties in a pre-emption proceeding is governed by section 96 (2), State. Acquisition and Tenancy Act. This section specifically provides that all co-sharer tenants, if preemption is sought by a co sharer, and all co-sharer tenants and all contiguous land holders, if pre-emption is sought by a contiguous land holder "shall be made parties". Impleading of such persons will not however be necessary if they have lost their interests in the land to be pre-empted or if they have waived their right to the pre-emption. Neither of these two ingredients is present in instant case where a number of co-sharers were omitted and the omission was not supplied even when opportunity was given. The High Court Division is found to bays erroneously held that the “left-out co-sharers" got no subsisting right of pre-emption, they are necessary parties and the non-joinder of these parties is fatal to the application for pre-emption.
